## TL;DR

The worktree-GC implementation is complete, and I re-verified every finding from review pass 1 against the current tree rather than trusting the earlier summary. This recovery round had one job left after the failed handoff: restore the engineering report draft the server had already consumed, re-run the scoped check on a fresh tree, and record the two remaining infrastructure blockers. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passes on the committed tree. The first is that review pass 2 was lost to a reviewer timeout, not a code defect. The second is that `repoos landable` on `main` misclassifies the task's own generated engineering report as another task's bookkeeping, so no task with a report can currently pass that check.

## Work and rationale

I checked all three pass-1 bugs in the shipped code. Committed task files are compared byte-for-byte with `main`, so a path match alone never makes a task file disposable. Rename detection is disabled in both contribution comparisons, so a rename is checked as an addition and a deletion instead of only the new path. Lifecycle state fails closed: an unreadable durable close-out store or an unbuildable task index skips the sweep, and a live worktree with no task record is retained rather than reclaimed.

I also confirmed the supporting behaviour the acceptance criteria ask for. `repoos gc --dry-run`, `repoos status`, and the automatic sweep all call the same function with the same inputs, so their candidate/retained/external counts cannot drift. The tests cover merged-and-clean branches, task-file-only dirt, unmerged commits, dirty source files, archived-ready tasks, active tasks, human-owned tasks, and unique noncanonical task content. The docs describe the automatic policy and where it refuses to act.

The handoff failure itself was not a source problem. The report draft had been deleted after the earlier report was committed, and the reused check inputs no longer matched the handoff tree. I rewrote the draft and re-ran the check against a clean tree, which is the recovery the server expects.

## Approaches tried

I considered deleting the committed round-1 report from the branch to get past the landable task-scope failure. I rejected that: the report is required review context, and handoff would immediately finalize and commit a new round, recreating the same state.

I also considered adding the landable exemption in this branch. It is a small, real fix — allow `work/engineering-reports/<own task id>/` in `isForbiddenTaskScopePath`, with a test — but the running server and CLI use `main`, so the change here cannot affect the current review and would be out-of-scope for a worktree-GC task. It should be its own small fix on `main`.

I did not merge `main` into the branch. Landable reports only this task's own task-file conflict, which close-out resolves from `main`, and the engineer sandbox deliberately does not commit.

## Challenges and blockers

Review pass 2 used `opencode/opencode-go/mimo-v2.6-flash` and timed out after 900 seconds with no report; it needs a retry with a different reviewer agent. Separately, `repoos landable 1004` and `repoos landable 0997` both fail task scope on their own engineering-report JSON. That is a systemic bug in the engineering-report feature's interaction with the landing checklist, not a defect in this branch. The existing review code already treats `work/engineering-reports/<id>/` as bookkeeping when it matches the reviewed tree, so the landable rule simply needs the same classification.

## Key learnings

Fail-closed cleanup needs positive lifecycle proof: "main already has these bytes" says nothing about whether an agent still owns the worktree. Generated bookkeeping also has to be classified once and allowed consistently at every gate; when review treats a report as bookkeeping but landable treats it as foreign drift, the gate becomes impossible to pass. I will report the landable fix as a follow-up rather than smuggling it into this task.
